sections.h2: How can I sell a house in McDonough, GA?
sections.html:
A McDonough owner has three practical paths: list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer on the house in its current shape. Each trades price against time and effort in a different way.

  • Agent sale: the widest buyer pool, and a closing timeline driven by the buyer's financing.
  • Owner sale: no agent on your side of the deal, so you handle pricing, paperwork and walk-throughs.
  • Cash purchase: fewer contingencies and no repair demands, which helps with inherited houses, tenant problems or payments that have fallen behind.

Whichever you choose, get the offer terms in writing, including who pays the Georgia transfer tax and how property tax is handled at closing.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show about McDonough's housing market?
sections.html:
McDonough has grown quickly. The Census Bureau counted 22,084 residents in 2010 and 29,051 in 2020, and it estimates 33,395 for July 1, 2025, which is 14.5% above the April 2020 estimates base of 29,178. The city covers 12.85 square miles of land, with 2,260.4 people per square mile in 2020.

  • Share of homes lived in by their owners, 2020 to 2024: 54.8%.
  • Median value of those homes: $314,600.
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $1,791.
  • Median gross rent: $1,792, a little above the monthly cost of owning with a mortgage.
  • Households: 10,886, averaging 2.76 people.
  • Median household income: $75,343.
  • Residents under 18: 26.4%; age 65 and over: 8.8%.
  • Adults 25 and over with a bachelor's degree or higher: 28.5%.
  • Households with a broadband subscription: 95.6%.
  • Mean commute: 32.5 minutes, longer than the 27.5 minutes listed for Marietta and 28.0 for Milton.

The age mix is young: more than a quarter of residents are under 18. A seller with a family-sized house can note that the Census lists 2.76 persons per household here, against 2.40 in Marietta.

sections.h2: What is McDonough's history and why does it matter to a seller?
sections.html:
McDonough is the seat of Henry County, about thirty miles southeast of Atlanta. According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia it was incorporated on December 17, 1823, and named for a naval hero of the War of 1812. The town was laid out in blocks with the courthouse originally in the center, near a water source called the Big Spring.

Early businesses served farmers: blacksmith shops, sawmills, grist mills and cotton gins, and the town served as a relay stop on the stagecoach line from New York to New Orleans. By 1921 a hydroelectric plant on the river supplied the city's electricity. Landmarks still standing include the Brown House, begun in 1826, and the Davis-Bryan-Hazlehurst House from around 1829. The city hosts the Geranium Festival in May and the Henry County Fair in the fall.

The McDonough Main Street Program, established in June 2001, works on revitalizing the older business district around the Square, with an office at 5 Griffin Street.

sections.h2: What permits and inspections does the City of McDonough require?
sections.html:
McDonough's Building and Inspection Division reviews plans and issues permits so that construction meets municipal code. The city says a permit is required to construct, enlarge, alter, repair, move or demolish a building, and to install, alter or replace electrical, gas, mechanical, plumbing or sprinkler systems. Georgia law, O.C.G.A. 43-14, requires licensed trades for plumbing, electrical and heating-air work, and the city states the same applies to homeowners doing that work themselves.

The city enforces the current Georgia State Minimum Codes for Construction as published by the Department of Community Affairs. The list includes the International Residential Code, the International Energy Conservation Code, the National Electrical Code and the International Property Maintenance Code. Water and sewer tap applications and an irrigation meter application are on the same division's forms page, and an Owner Occupied Housing Rehabilitation Program application is listed there too.

Code Compliance sits inside the Planning and Zoning Division of Community Development. The city notes that the Mayor and Council adopt the codes but do not handle individual compliance cases. Code Compliance officers usually notify the person responsible, explain how to fix the violation and allow a set time. If voluntary efforts fail, a citation sends the matter to McDonough Municipal Court.

Before listing, check that decks, water heaters, additions or finished basements were permitted. The city says work done without the proper permits can be penalized, and a buyer's inspector may ask for proof.

sections.h2: How do Henry County assessments and appeals affect a McDonough sale?
sections.html:
Henry County's Tax Assessor pages cover the Notice of Assessment, Property Appeals, Homestead Exemption, Conservation Use and Property Returns. Georgia's appeal statute, O.C.G.A. 48-5-311, is the state framework, and the Macon-Bibb assessors' summary of it explains that a written appeal is due within 45 days of the notice date. The same statewide process applies to a McDonough owner, so read the date printed on your own notice.

Because the notice shows the assessed value and an estimate of taxes, it is worth keeping with your sale papers. Ask the Henry County Tax Commissioner for your current bill, due dates and any balance before you set a closing date, and ask the Tax Assessor which exemptions your house carries. A homestead exemption belongs to the seller and ends at the sale, so the buyer files a new application for their own exemption after closing.

sections.h2: What transfer tax and recording steps apply in McDonough?
sections.html:
Henry County's Clerk of Superior Court records deeds, and the real estate transfer tax must be paid first. The Department of Revenue prints the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 or fractional part of $1,000, and 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part of $100.

The seller is liable under O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10, although many sales contracts make the buyer pay. The PT-61 declaration is completed online with the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority and a copy goes to the Clerk with the deed. Ask the Henry County Clerk about exemptions.

faqs.q: Can I sell a McDonough house that has an open code violation?
faqs.a: Yes, though the cleanest path is to resolve it first. McDonough's Code Compliance Division normally gives the responsible person time to fix a violation and cites them to Municipal Court if that fails. Report or ask about a case through the hotline at 470-878-1150.

faqs.q: How soon can I get a building inspection in McDonough?
faqs.a: Call the inspection request line at 678-782-6217 before 4 p.m. for a next-day inspection. Requests after 4 p.m. are scheduled two days out, and Friday or holiday calls before 4 p.m. go to the next working day.

faqs.q: How much is McDonough's median home value?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau lists $314,600 as the median value of owner-occupied housing units for 2020 to 2024, and 54.8% of homes are owner-occupied. Actual prices for your house depend on its condition and street.

faqs.q: Who pays the Georgia transfer tax in a McDonough sale?
faqs.a: The seller is liable under the statute, and many contracts shift it to the buyer. The state rate is $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each extra $100 or fraction. Check your contract and ask the Henry County Clerk of Superior Court about exemptions.

faqs.q: What should I ask Henry County before closing on my McDonough house?
faqs.a: Ask the Tax Commissioner for the current bill and any balance, and ask the Tax Assessor which exemptions apply. Also confirm whether your house is inside McDonough's city limits, since city permit and code rules apply only there.
